c.reason: EUR 8.11 billion applies a flat 18% to the entire BI and then the ILM: $56.0 \times 0.18 \times 0.8050$. The top coefficient is used as an average rate.

d.reason: EUR 9.15 billion is the BIC itself, with the ILM never applied. It is a legitimate intermediate quantity of the correct calculation, not the capital charge.

trap.explanation: (d) is an intermediate-result trap, and the most dangerous option, because the BIC is computed correctly on the way to the answer and a candidate who stops after the marginal-coefficient work will select it. (a) and (c) are wrong input twins, substituting an average coefficient for the marginal schedule, at the bottom and top of the range respectively. Note the two-stage discipline this item rewards: the marginal build first, the multiplier second, and only then the 12.5 conversion. Note also that the source distractors could not all be traced to a named operator, so two were rebuilt on the trap library; the stem and correct answer are unchanged.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate the Standardised Approach and the operational risk capital requirement.
questions.reading: Chapter 2 (Risk Governance), Ch 2.2c; Chapter 24 (Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms, BCBS December 2017), Ch 24.2
questions.topic: The Internal Loss Multiplier and the Loss Component
questions.question: A supervisor is reviewing a bank whose Business Indicator Component is EUR 2.67 billion and whose average annual operational risk losses over the previous ten years have been EUR 200 million. The national regulator has not exercised its discretion to set the Internal Loss Multiplier equal to one. Which of the following is nearest to the bank's operational risk capital charge?

options.text: EUR 1.56 billion
EUR 2.67 billion
EUR 2.79 billion
EUR 3.00 billion

questions.solution:
Step 1, the Loss Component. The Loss Component is 15 times average annual operational risk losses incurred over the previous ten years:

$$LC = 15 \times 0.200 = \text{EUR } 3.00 \text{ billion}$$

Step 2, the ratio.

$$\frac{LC}{BIC} = \frac{3.00}{2.67} = 1.1236$$

Because LC exceeds BIC, the ILM must be greater than one before any arithmetic is done: a bank with losses that are high relative to its BIC is required to hold higher capital.

Step 3, the Internal Loss Multiplier.

$$ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + \frac{LC}{BIC}\right] = \ln[2.71828 - 1 + 1.1236] = \ln[2.84188] = 1.0445$$

Step 4, the capital charge.

$$ORC = BIC \times ILM = 2.67 \times 1.0445 = \text{EUR } 2.7889 \text{ billion, or nearest EUR } 2.79 \text{ billion}$$

Behavioural check. The formula is constructed so that:

$$LC = BIC \implies \frac{LC}{BIC} = 1 \implies ILM = \ln[e] = 1$$
$$LC > BIC \implies ILM > 1 \implies \text{higher capital}$$
$$LC < BIC \implies ILM < 1 \implies \text{lower capital}$$

Two framework qualifications matter. Banks with fewer than five years of high-quality loss data must calculate the requirement solely on the Business Indicator Component, and banks that fail the loss data standards must hold capital at a minimum equal to 100% of the BIC, with supervisors able to require an ILM greater than one. Separately, the ILM has been left to national discretion, so a supervisor may set it equal to one for all banks in the jurisdiction, in which case ORC simply equals BIC. The stem rules that discretion out.

a.reason: EUR 1.56 billion omits the factor of 15 in the Loss Component, treating LC as EUR 0.20 billion. That gives LC/BIC of 0.0749 and an ILM of 0.584, producing a capital charge far below the BIC.

b.reason: EUR 2.67 billion is the BIC, that is the answer if the ILM is set to one. The stem states the national discretion has not been exercised, and in any case LC exceeds BIC so the multiplier cannot be one.

c.reason: EUR 2.79 billion, from BIC times the correctly computed ILM.

d.reason: EUR 3.00 billion is the Loss Component itself. It also happens to be the result of using the raw ratio LC divided by BIC as the multiplier instead of running it through the logarithm, since 2.67 multiplied by 1.1236 returns 3.00.

trap.explanation: (d) is an intermediate-result trap with a second route into it: the Loss Component is a legitimate intermediate quantity, and the naive multiplier of LC divided by BIC arrives at the same figure, which makes the option doubly attractive. The logarithm exists precisely to damp the adjustment, so a bank whose losses run 12% above its BIC faces a capital uplift of about 4.5%, not 12%. (a) is a dropped term, omitting the multiple of 15. (b) is a wrong input twin, substituting the BIC for the ORC by assuming the ILM equals one; note the stem plants the national discretion sentence specifically to test whether you read it. A useful sanity check before computing: establish the direction from the LC versus BIC comparison first, then verify that your arithmetic moves the capital the same way.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Compare the SMA to earlier methods including the AMA.
questions.reading: Chapter 2 (Risk Governance), Ch 2.2c
questions.topic: The three Basel II approaches
questions.question:
You are helping your bank understand the approaches to operational risk capital that applied before January 2023. You ask a colleague for a brief summary of the differences between the three approaches, and he replies with the following three statements:

I. In the basic indicator approach, total capital is 25% of last year's annual revenue.

II. In the standardised approach, gross income is calculated for different business lines, and capital as a percentage of gross income differs across business lines.

III. In the advanced measurement approach, the bank uses internal models to determine the 99.9% one-year value at risk.

Which of the above is or are correct?

options.text: None are correct
I only
II and III only
All are correct

questions.solution:
| Approach | Base | Rate | Discretion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic Indicator Approach (BIA) | Average yearly gross income over the past three years, with years of negative or zero gross income excluded | 15%, the alpha factor | None. Not intended for internationally active banks or banks with significant operational risk exposures |
| Standardised Approach (TSA) | Gross income separated by business line | 12%, 15% or 18%, the beta factors, depending on the perceived riskiness of the underlying business line | None on the rates; the split is prescribed |
| Advanced Measurement Approaches (AMA), and Internal Modeling Approaches (IMA) for insurers | The bank's own modelled loss distribution | Capital sufficient to cover all possible operational losses up to a 99.9% confidence interval at a one-year horizon, that is losses in 999 out of 1000 simulated years | Full, subject to validation of the model and framework by the regulator of each country of incorporation |

Statement I is false on both the rate and the base. The alpha factor is 15%, not 25%, and it is applied to the three-year average of gross income, not to last year's revenue. Gross income is defined as net interest income plus net non-interest income as defined by national supervisors or national accounting standards.

Statement II is true. This is exactly the business-line beta structure of TSA. Note that the later SA reform departed from this view, because operational losses incurred in banks' various lines of business over the past twenty years did not match the expectations embedded in the betas.

Statement III is true.

a.reason: Statements II and III are both accurate.

b.reason: Statement I is the one false statement of the three.

c.reason: Statements II and III are correct; statement I is false.

d.reason: Statement I misstates both the rate and the base.

trap.explanation: Statement I carries two independent corruptions in a single sentence, which is what makes it dangerous: a candidate who checks only the rate, or only the base, may pass it. The first is a wrong input twin on the rate, 25% substituted for the 15% alpha factor, with 25% being close enough to be unmemorable as wrong. The second is a scope or condition error on the base, one year substituted for a three-year average, which also silently drops the rule excluding negative and zero gross income years. Fix the numbers as a triple: BIA is 15% of a three-year average; TSA is 12, 15 or 18 per cent by business line; AMA is a 99.9% one-year internal model.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Compare the SMA to earlier methods including the AMA.
questions.reading: Chapter 24 (Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms, BCBS December 2017), Ch 24
questions.topic: The December 2017 Basel III revisions
questions.question: The December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework included changes in several areas, among them credit risk, counterparty credit valuation adjustment risk, operational risk, the leverage ratio and a revised output floor. In regard to these revisions, each of the following is true EXCEPT which one?

options.text: For counterparty credit risk, the credit valuation adjustment framework was revised to enhance its risk sensitivity, strengthen its robustness and improve its consistency.
For operational risk, the previous standardised approaches and the internal approach were replaced by a single risk-sensitive standardised approach to be used by all banks.
For operational risk, the new approach eliminated the bank's historical internal loss experience as an input, because that experience was observed to be uncorrelated with actual operational losses.

With respect to the revised output floor, a bank's risk-weighted assets calculated under internal models cannot be lower than 72.5% of the total risk-weighted assets calculated using only the standardised approaches.

questions.solution:
Statement (c) is false and inverts the central design feature of the new approach. Internal loss experience is retained, and it enters the calculation through the Internal Loss Multiplier:

$$ORC = BIC \times ILM, \qquad ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + \frac{LC}{BIC}\right], \qquad LC = 15 \times \text{average annual operational risk losses over the previous 10 years}$$

A bank's internal operational risk loss experience therefore affects the calculation of operational risk capital directly. A bank with losses that are high relative to its BIC is required to hold higher capital, and conversely a bank with low losses relative to its BIC holds lower capital.

What the reform did eliminate is the internal model, not the internal loss data. Statement (b) states this correctly: the standardised approach for measuring minimum operational risk capital requirements replaces all existing approaches in the Basel II framework, that is BIA, TSA and AMA are all superseded by a single approach applying to internationally active banks on a consolidated basis, with supervisors retaining discretion to apply it to non-internationally active banks.

Two qualifications on the loss input are worth holding, because they are the nearest true statements to the false one in (c). Banks in bucket 1, with a BI at or below EUR 1 billion, have their ILM set to one, so internal loss data does not affect their capital calculation. And the ILM has been left to national discretion, so a supervisor may set it equal to one for all banks in the jurisdiction. Neither of those is the same as eliminating loss experience from the framework.

a.reason: True, so not the answer. The CVA framework revision is one of the named areas.

b.reason: True, so not the answer. A single approach replaced the previous menu.

c.reason: False, and therefore the answer. Loss experience is retained through the ILM.

d.reason: True, so not the answer. The output floor sets internally modelled RWA at no less than 72.5% of the standardised total.

trap.explanation: (c) is a polarity flip on whether loss data was retained or removed, supported by a manufactured justification that sounds like a plausible empirical finding. It is attractive because the reform genuinely did remove internal modelling, so a candidate who remembers "internal something was abolished" will accept it. Separate the two words: the reform abolished the internal model and kept the internal loss data. The national-discretion and bucket-1 carve-outs are the true statements this distractor is built to be confused with.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Compare the SMA to earlier methods including the AMA.
questions.reading: Chapter 2 (Risk Governance), Ch 2.2c; Chapter 24 (Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms, BCBS December 2017)
questions.topic: Why the SMA replaced the AMA
questions.question: A regulatory affairs analyst is preparing a note for her bank's audit committee explaining how the Standardised Approach compares with the approaches it replaced. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The SMA is less risk-sensitive than the BIA and the TSA, because it replaces gross income with a business indicator that ignores the composition of a bank's revenue.
The SMA retains the AMA's core feature of allowing each bank to model its own capital requirement, but standardises the confidence level at 99.9% over a one-year horizon.

The SMA is a single approach applied to all banks in place of a three-tier menu, it retains sensitivity to a bank's own experience through the Internal Loss Multiplier rather than through an internal model, and its marginal coefficients rise with size on the view that operational risk grows more than proportionally with the scale of the organisation.
The SMA raises capital requirements for all banks relative to the AMA, because the removal of internal modelling eliminates every source of capital relief.

questions.solution:
| Feature | BIA | TSA | AMA | SMA / SA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | Three-year average gross income | Gross income by business line | Modelled loss distribution | Business Indicator, a broader financial-statement proxy |
| Rate | Flat 15% alpha | 12, 15 or 18 per cent beta by business line | Bank's own model output | 12, 15 or 18 per cent marginal coefficient by size bucket |
| Sensitivity to own experience | None | None | Through the internal model | Through the Internal Loss Multiplier, using ten years of loss data |
| Bank discretion | None | None | Full, subject to regulatory validation | None on method; national discretion on whether the ILM applies |

Why the change. The 2007 to 2009 financial crisis left operational risk rules untouched for a while, and in 2015 the Basel Committee began working on a reform of Pillar 1 capital for operational risk. The work led to the December 2017 update, which discontinued the three-tier regulatory capital regime and introduced a single measure effective from January 2023 with transitional regimes until January 2025. The SA reform also departed from the TSA's business-line view, because operational losses incurred in banks' various lines of business over the past twenty years did not match the expectations embedded in the beta factors.

Why the coefficients rise with size. By increasing the percentages with the size of the bank, regulators have recognised that the level of operational risk increases more than proportionally with size: the larger the organisation, the more complex the processes, operations and interactions, and that extra complexity should be covered by additional funds.

Direction of the capital effect. The SMA does not mechanically raise capital for every bank. The ILM cuts both ways, and a bank whose Loss Component is below its Business Indicator Component receives an ILM below one and therefore a reduction, as at Q33.

a.reason: The Business Indicator is a broader proxy than gross income, not a narrower one, and the SMA adds a loss-experience input that neither BIA nor TSA had. Statement (b) of Q36 describes the new approach as risk-sensitive for exactly this reason.

b.reason: The SMA removes bank modelling entirely. The 99.9% one-year confidence level belongs to the AMA and does not appear in the SMA at all.

c.reason: One approach for everyone, loss sensitivity kept through the ILM rather than a model, and coefficients that escalate with size.

d.reason: The ILM is symmetric: it is greater than one when LC exceeds BIC and less than one when LC is below BIC, so banks with low loss experience relative to their business size receive relief.

trap.explanation: (b) is a sibling swap, importing the AMA's defining parameter into the SMA and preserving the very feature the reform abolished. (a) is a polarity flip on risk sensitivity, and it is tempting because "standardised" intuitively suggests "cruder". (d) is an absolute-claim trap on "all banks" and "every source of capital relief", defeated by the symmetry of the ILM. The three-sentence summary to carry: one approach for everyone, loss sensitivity kept but through a multiplier rather than a model, and coefficients that escalate with size because complexity escalates faster than scale.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
questions.reading: Chapter 8 (Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices, BCBS 2018), Ch 8.4
questions.topic: Diagnosing a failed recovery
questions.question: Capital Bank has suffered a serious system breach resulting in the loss of sensitive customer data. The information security department is attempting to restore systems and locate critical data back-ups, but nobody appears to know exactly what they are supposed to do. The bank has a rapid recovery plan in place, but the relevant personnel do not know what protocol to follow when executing it, and the recovery team is struggling to coordinate its work. Which vulnerability is most likely to blame?

options.text: Failure to conduct a business impact analysis
Failure to back up sensitive data adequately
Failure to establish an alternate processing site
Failure to test the disaster recovery strategy

questions.solution:
Read the symptoms rather than the topic. The stem reports three things: a plan exists; personnel do not know the protocol; and the team cannot coordinate. Each wrong option would produce a different symptom.

| If this had failed | The symptom would have been | Matches stem? |
|---|---|---|
| Business impact analysis | Wrong recovery priorities, restoring low-criticality services first | No |
| Data back-up | Data irrecoverably lost | No, back-ups exist and are being located |
| Alternate site | Nowhere to run recovered operations from | No |
| Testing the recovery strategy | Plan exists, roles unrehearsed, coordination fails | Yes |

The curriculum is emphatic on this point. Most regulators and international standards expect financial institutions to test protective measures periodically, and advanced regulators require tests for critical activities to be based on realistic and probable disruptive scenarios, conducted at least annually, with service providers and significant counterparties involved through collaborative and coordinated resilience testing. Distinct from testing, most supervisors and banks also use exercises to train and practise how they would respond to an incident.

This item absorbs a second source question that asked which activity is most critical before a newly developed continuity plan is finalised and implemented. The answer there is continuity testing, for the same reason: tests validate whether services can in fact be restored within the stipulated timelines.

a.reason: A missing business impact analysis would show up as mis-prioritised recovery, not role confusion. The BIA has in fact done its job here, since the team knows which data is critical and is looking for it.

b.reason: The stem says the team is locating back-ups, so back-ups exist.

c.reason: An alternate site addresses where to run, not who does what.

d.reason: Failure to test the disaster recovery strategy is most likely to blame.

trap.explanation: (a) is a sibling swap and the trap for a candidate who pattern-matches on vocabulary, since "business impact analysis" is the most technical-sounding term in the option set and appears constantly in this topic. (b) and (c) are scope or condition errors, each proposing a failure the stem has already ruled out. The discipline that defeats all three is to match each candidate cause to the symptom it would produce and check that symptom against the stem, rather than picking the cause that sounds most fundamental.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
questions.reading: Chapter 8 (Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices, BCBS 2018), Ch 8.3
questions.topic: Resolving a disagreement over a risk assessment
questions.question: Exim Bank has just completed a risk assessment and business impact analysis with respect to cyber-attacks and the latest emerging threats and vulnerabilities in cyberspace. However, the bank's information security manager and its business department manager do not agree on who will ultimately be responsible for the detailed evaluation of the results and the risk analysis. Which of the following would be the best course of action in these circumstances?

options.text: Acceptance and implementation of the information security manager's decision on the risk to the bank.
Acceptance and implementation of the business department manager's decision on the risk to the bank.
Creation of a new risk assessment and business impact analysis in order to iron out the differences.
Review of the report with senior management for final input.

questions.solution:
Senior management and executives play a pivotal role in the evaluation and management of cyber risk, and this is emphasised in the Basel Committee's range of practices report. As with other risk types, senior management is ultimately responsible for promoting and maintaining cyber-resilience within the institution, and it has both the authority and the responsibility to resolve issues arising during implementation.

The structural reason (a) and (b) fail is that neither manager can settle the question, because the disagreement is about who owns the evaluation, and neither party can arbitrate its own claim. The information security manager sits in a control function and the business department manager sits in the first line, so allowing either to impose its view either strips the business of ownership of its own risk or strips the control function of its challenge role.

Escalating to senior management resolves it at the level with the authority to allocate the responsibility, and it ensures the decision reflects the overall strategic objectives and risk appetite of the organisation, which is a judgement neither manager is positioned to make alone.

a.reason: Allowing the information security manager to impose a decision makes a control function the risk owner, which inverts the principle that risk is owned by the business where it is generated.

b.reason: Allowing the business manager to impose a decision removes the independent challenge that the security function exists to provide.

c.reason: Redoing the assessment addresses neither party's objection, since the dispute is about ownership of the evaluation rather than about the quality of the analysis. It also consumes time during which the identified exposures remain unmanaged.

d.reason: Review of the report with senior management for final input resolves the dispute at the level with the authority to allocate responsibility.

trap.explanation: (a) and (b) are role misassignments, each handing arbitration to one of the disputing parties, and both are attractive because each manager has a genuine claim to expertise in the matter. (c) is a scope or condition error, treating an ownership dispute as an analytical dispute. The general rule this item rewards is that when two parties at the same organisational level disagree about accountability, the resolution is always escalation to the level that can assign it, never a contest between the parties.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Model risk and how it arises in implementation. Describe, explain
questions.reading: Chapter 15.3, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
questions.topic: What model risk is and why it arises
questions.question: A model risk manager at a large bank is briefing a new intake of analysts on the supervisory definition of model risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports, and it arises primarily for two reasons: the model may have fundamental errors producing inaccurate outputs, or the model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately.
Model risk is the risk that a model takes longer to build or costs more to implement than budgeted, and it is therefore principally a project management concern.
Model risk is the risk that a model produces outputs that differ from those of a competitor's model for the same exposure, and it is eliminated once benchmarking against peer models is performed.
Model risk arises only from errors in the mathematical processing component, since input data quality is addressed separately under data governance and reporting is a presentational matter.

questions.solution:
The SR 11-7 definition of model risk and its two primary sources is the anchor definition for the whole model risk topic.

The use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports. Model risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or damage to a bank's reputation.

Model risk occurs primarily for TWO reasons:

1. The model may have FUNDAMENTAL ERRORS and produce inaccurate outputs when viewed against its design objective and intended business uses.
2. The model may be USED INCORRECTLY or INAPPROPRIATELY, or its limitations or assumptions may be poorly understood.

The two sources matter because they call for different responses. Fundamental error is addressed through development discipline, testing and validation. Incorrect use is addressed through governance, documentation, user training and the clear statement of a model's limitations. A bank that validates rigorously but allows its models to be applied outside their intended scope has controlled only half the risk.

Note that models are simplified representations of real-world relationships. Simplification is inevitable, because those relationships are inherently complex, and it is also intentional, in order to focus attention on the aspects considered most important for a given application. Models are never perfect, and the appropriate metrics of quality depend on the situation: precision and accuracy are relevant for models that forecast future values, while discriminatory power applies to models that rank order risks.

a.reason: Definition plus both primary sources.

b.reason: Cost and delivery overruns are project risk. Model risk concerns the consequences of decisions taken on model output, not the cost of building the model.

c.reason: Benchmarking against alternative approaches is one validation activity, not a definition of model risk, and it does not eliminate anything. Two models can agree and both be wrong.

d.reason: A model has three components, input, processing and reporting, and error or misuse in any of them creates model risk. Poor input data and a misleading report are model risk, not adjacent risks.

trap.explanation: (b) is a sibling swap, substituting project risk for model risk, and it is the option a candidate picks by reasoning about what could go wrong with a modelling project rather than with a model. (c) is an absolute-claim trap on "eliminated". (d) is a scope or condition error, narrowing model risk to one of the three model components. The rebuild preserves the concept and adds the second source of model risk, which is the half candidates forget.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Model risk and how it arises in implementation. Describe, explain
questions.reading: Chapter 15.3 and Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.topic: How model risk arises in implementation
questions.question: A model validation lead is reviewing a newly deployed credit scoring model. Which of the following is most likely to be a source of model risk arising specifically at the implementation stage rather than at the design stage?

options.text: The theoretical framework underlying the scoring methodology is not supported by the academic literature for the borrower population concerned.
The model has been coded correctly but is being applied to a portfolio segment materially different from the development sample, and the users are unaware of the limitation.
The chosen functional form fails to capture a non-linearity that is known to exist in the relationship being modelled.
The confidence level selected for the model output does not correspond to the bank's stated risk appetite.

questions.solution:
SR 11-7's two sources of model risk map onto two different stages.

| Source | Stage | Typical manifestation |
|---|---|---|
| Fundamental error in the model | Design and development | Wrong theory, wrong functional form, sample design flaws, unsupported assumptions, coding errors |
| Incorrect or inappropriate use | Implementation and use | Application outside the intended scope or population, users unaware of limitations, output fed into a decision the model was never built to support, stale recalibration |

Option (b) describes a model that is internally sound and correctly coded but is being applied to a population it was not developed for, with users unaware. That is the classic implementation-stage failure, and it is why SR 11-7 requires a clear statement of purpose to ensure model development is aligned with the intended use, and why documentation must record the model's limitations so that users understand them.

Note the practical asymmetry the case study material draws out: sample bias in model data is described as a common error in model use and management across all industries, not just financial services, and it is precisely the error that survives a technically clean build.

a.reason: An unsupported theoretical framework is a conceptual soundness failure, which sits at the design stage and is caught by qualitative review of documentation and derivation.

c.reason: Functional form selection is a design choice.

d.reason: Calibration of a confidence level to risk appetite is a design and policy parameter decision, settled before the model is built.

trap.explanation: (a), (c) and (d) are scope or condition errors, each offering a genuine source of model risk located at the wrong stage. The stem's discriminating word is implementation, and the test is whether the candidate can separate "the model is wrong" from "the model is fine but is being used wrongly". A useful diagnostic: if fixing the problem would require rebuilding the model, it is a design failure; if it would require changing who uses it, on what, and with what warnings, it is an implementation failure.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Elements of an effective model risk management process. Describe
questions.reading: Chapter 15, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
questions.topic: The three elements of model risk management
questions.question: A bank is building a model risk management framework in line with supervisory guidance. Which of the following best describes the elements that framework should contain?

options.text: Robust model development, implementation and use; a sound model validation process; and governance, policies and controls, all underpinned by effective challenge from parties with the incentive, competence and influence to act.
A single centralised validation team that both develops and validates all models, so that the deepest technical expertise in the bank is applied at both stages.
An annual internal audit review of the model inventory, which discharges the bank's obligations because internal audit is the independent third line of defence.
A requirement that all models be sourced from external vendors, since vendor models carry the vendor's own validation and therefore transfer model risk out of the bank.

questions.solution:
Model risk management framework, three elements:

1. Robust model DEVELOPMENT, IMPLEMENTATION and USE
2. Sound model VALIDATION
3. GOVERNANCE, POLICIES and CONTROLS

Guiding principle throughout: EFFECTIVE CHALLENGE, meaning critical analysis by objective, informed parties who can identify model limitations and assumptions and produce appropriate change. Effective challenge depends on a combination of INCENTIVES, COMPETENCE and INFLUENCE.

The guidance is explicit that model risk should be managed like other types of risk: the bank should identify the sources of risk and assess their magnitude, and management should ensure the level of model risk is within the bank's tolerance and take action to reduce it where it is not.

The three elements are complementary rather than substitutable, which is what defeats options (b), (c) and (d). Validation without development discipline means finding errors late. Development discipline without governance means no one is accountable for acting on what validation finds.

b.reason: Combining development and validation in one team destroys the independence on which effective challenge depends. Model developers must not be members of the validation team for the models they built.

c.reason: Internal audit's role is to assess the overall effectiveness of the model risk management framework, not to perform validation. Substituting audit for validation collapses the second and third lines and leaves the framework itself unaudited.

d.reason: Vendor models are a recognised source of model risk, not a transfer of it. Vendor products should be subject to the same validation and governance as in-house models, and the bank remains responsible for their appropriate use, which is harder because vendor methodology is often proprietary and opaque.

trap.explanation: (b) and (c) are role misassignments, collapsing two distinct functions into one; (c) is the more attractive because it invokes the genuinely correct principle of third-line independence and then applies it to the wrong task. (d) is an absolute-claim trap on transferring risk out of the bank, and the same accountability-transfer fallacy that appears in the outsourcing and third-party objectives.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Elements of an effective model risk management process. Describe
questions.reading: Chapter 15, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
questions.topic: The core elements of model validation
questions.question: A risk management team is implementing a comprehensive validation framework for newly developed credit risk models in preparation for regulatory review. Which validation activity is most appropriate for determining whether the mathematical framework of the model is conceptually well founded?

options.text: Qualitative review of model documentation and the derivation of the formulae, together with comparison against established theoretical frameworks and alternative approaches.
Data quality checks focusing on the completeness, accuracy and appropriateness of input data.
Systems implementation testing, including user acceptance testing and code verification.
Management oversight in which senior leadership reviews model outputs and their application in business decisions.

questions.solution:
Every option describes a real validation or control activity, so the discrimination is entirely about matching activity to purpose.

| Core element of validation | Question it answers | Typical activity |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluation of conceptual soundness | Is the model theoretically well founded and appropriate for its purpose? | Qualitative review of documentation, developmental evidence and derivation of formulae; comparison with published theory and with alternative approaches; assessment of the quality of the design and construction |
| Ongoing monitoring | Is the model still working as intended in the current environment? | Process verification, benchmarking, sensitivity analysis to changing conditions |
| Outcomes analysis | Do the model's outputs match what actually happened? | Back-testing, comparison of forecasts to realised values |

Conceptual soundness is the element that asks whether the mathematics is well founded in the first place, which is what the stem asks for. Note the guidance also expects developers to compare their models with alternative approaches and theories and to explain the merits and limitations of the chosen methodology and its processing components.

a.reason: This is conceptual soundness.

b.reason: Data quality is a genuine and required validation activity, and poor data is a real source of model risk, but it tests the inputs, not whether the mathematical framework is sound. A conceptually flawed model fed with perfect data is still flawed.

c.reason: Implementation testing verifies that the code does what the specification says. It cannot tell you whether the specification was right.

d.reason: Management oversight belongs to governance, the third element of the framework, not to validation, and reviewing outputs after the fact is closer to outcomes analysis than to conceptual review.

trap.explanation: All three distractors are role misassignments, offering a real activity performed for a different purpose. The defence is to ask what each activity could possibly detect. Code verification cannot detect a wrong theory; data checks cannot detect a wrong functional form; management review cannot detect either. Only a qualitative review of the derivation against established theory can, which is why conceptual soundness is always the first core element listed.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Elements of an effective model risk management process. Describe
questions.reading: Chapter 15, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
questions.topic: Independence in the validation process
questions.question: A bank's head of model risk is reviewing the composition and reporting of its validation function. Which of the following is NOT consistent with supervisory guidance on model validation?

options.text: Documentation should record the circumstances in which the internal model does not work effectively, so that users understand its limitations.
The developers of a model should also serve on the validation team for that model, so that the validation benefits from the deepest available understanding of the methodology.

Validation should be performed by staff with the requisite competence, and the party responsible for ensuring a model has undergone appropriate validation and approval before deployment is the model owner.
Use of vendor models is a recognised challenge for validation, because the vendor's methodology may be proprietary and the bank must still validate the model's appropriateness for its own use.

questions.solution:
Effective challenge requires critical analysis by objective, informed parties, and objectivity is lost the moment a developer validates their own work. The guidance is clear that model developers must not be part of the validation team for the models they built. What developers are responsible for is the quality of the build itself: a clear statement of purpose aligned with the intended use, rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance, and model testing.

```
Developer               -> statement of purpose, data quality, model testing
Independent validator   -> conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring,
                            outcomes analysis
Model owner             -> ensures validation and approval have occurred
                            BEFORE deployment
Internal audit          -> assesses whether the FRAMEWORK as a whole works
Board and senior mgmt   -> governance, policy, tolerance for model risk
```

The distinction in the third row is easy to miss. Independent validation performs the validation, but the model owner is the party primarily responsible for ensuring that it has been done and that approval has been obtained before the model is deployed. Ownership of the obligation is not the same as execution of the work.

a.reason: Consistent with supervisory guidance, so not the answer. Documenting where the model does not work effectively is a positive requirement, not an admission of failure.

b.reason: Not consistent with supervisory guidance, and therefore the answer. Developers on the validation team destroys independence.

c.reason: Consistent with supervisory guidance, so not the answer. Competence is required, and pre-deployment assurance is the model owner's responsibility.

d.reason: Consistent with supervisory guidance, so not the answer. Vendor models are explicitly identified as a validation challenge.

trap.explanation: (b) is a role misassignment dressed as a competence argument, which is what makes it plausible: developers really do understand their own model best. Independence beats familiarity, for the same reason internal audit may not design the framework it reviews. Note that (c) contains a second discrimination worth holding separately, between the party that performs validation and the party accountable for it having happened.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Define a model; ways firms become exposed to model risk. Define, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 15.3, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
questions.topic: What counts as a model
questions.question: A bank is compiling its model inventory and must decide which of its spreadsheets fall within the supervisory definition of a model. Which of the following best describes a model for these purposes?

options.text: A spreadsheet that aggregates the trading positions of several desks for reporting purposes.
A spreadsheet containing coded probabilistic risk calculations that allow what-if scenarios to be run each day.
Any spreadsheet used by more than one business unit, regardless of what it computes.
Any application whose inputs are entirely quantitative, since approaches relying on expert judgement fall outside the definition.

questions.solution:
A MODEL is a quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions to process INPUT DATA into QUANTITATIVE ESTIMATES.

Three components:

1. INFORMATION INPUT — delivers assumptions and data
2. PROCESSING — transforms inputs into estimates
3. REPORTING — translates estimates into useful business information

Two boundary rules follow. First, the definition turns on whether theories, techniques and assumptions are applied to produce an estimate. A tool that only aggregates or re-presents existing numbers is not applying a theory and is therefore not a model, however large or important it is. Second, the definition also covers quantitative approaches whose inputs are partly or wholly qualitative or based on expert judgement, provided the output is quantitative in nature.

Option (b) satisfies the definition: probabilistic calculation is the application of statistical technique, scenario capability means assumptions are being processed, and the output is a quantitative estimate.

a.reason: Aggregation for reporting applies no theory and generates no estimate. It re-presents data the bank already holds.

c.reason: Breadth of use is not a criterion. The definition is about what the tool does, not who uses it.

d.reason: This inverts the second boundary rule. The definition expressly extends to approaches with qualitative or expert-judgement inputs, provided the output is quantitative. A scorecard driven by expert weightings is a model.

trap.explanation: (d) is a scope or condition error, and the important one, because it narrows the inventory in exactly the direction that leaves expert-judgement scorecards and rating overlays unmanaged. (c) is a scope or condition error substituting a usage criterion for a functional one. (a) is a sibling swap between a reporting tool and a model. The one-line test to hold: does it apply a technique to produce a quantitative estimate? If yes it is a model, regardless of whether the inputs are hard data or judgement, and regardless of whether it lives in a spreadsheet or a vendor system.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Outsourcing risk and an effective outsourcing risk programme. Explain, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 12.2, 12.3, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: Risks arising from the use of service providers
questions.question: A US bank is considering outsourcing part of its operations to a third-party service provider. Which of the following statements about the risks that arise and about who bears them is most accurate?

options.text: Outsourcing transfers both the activity and the accountability for it, provided the contract expressly assigns responsibility for losses to the service provider.

The use of service providers can expose the bank to compliance, concentration, reputational, country, operational and legal risks, and the board and senior management remain responsible for ensuring outsourced activities are performed in a safe and sound manner and in compliance with applicable law.
Because service providers are commercial counterparties rather than borrowers, outsourcing creates no credit exposure of any kind and can be excluded from the bank's counterparty framework.
Risks from outsourcing are confined to the period after the contract is signed, so pre-contract due diligence is a commercial rather than a risk management activity.

questions.solution:
The guidance opens from the position that the use of service providers does not diminish the responsibility of the board of directors and senior management to ensure that the outsourced activity is performed in a safe and sound manner and in compliance with applicable law. A financial institution may outsource the activity; it never outsources the accountability.

| Risk category | How it arises through outsourcing |
|---|---|
| Compliance | The provider's processes are not consistent with law, regulation or the institution's own policies and ethical standards |
| Concentration | Reliance on a limited number of providers, or many activities placed with one provider, or geographic concentration of providers |
| Reputational | Poor service, provider misconduct or a provider data breach that customers attribute to the institution |
| Country | Where the provider is located abroad: political, social, legal and economic conditions in that jurisdiction |
| Operational | Failure of the provider's own processes, people, systems or external events, including business continuity failure |
| Legal | Exposure to litigation and to unenforceable or ambiguous contract terms |

Because the accountability stays with the institution, the guidance requires a service provider risk management programme built around risk assessments, due diligence and selection, contract provisions, incentive compensation review, oversight and monitoring, business continuity and contingency considerations, and additional risk considerations.

a.reason: A contractual allocation of loss may recover money; it does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility to a supervisor or a customer. This is the accountability-transfer fallacy.

c.reason: A provider's financial deterioration is a genuine exposure, which is exactly why financial condition review forms part of due diligence and ongoing monitoring.

d.reason: The programme begins with risk assessment and due diligence before selection. A provider chosen badly cannot be managed well afterwards.

trap.explanation: (a) is a role misassignment, and the single most examinable error in this topic: it recurs elsewhere, and in the cyber and model risk objectives. (c) and (d) are scope or condition errors, each excluding a period or a risk type from the programme. Hold the sentence verbatim: the use of service providers does not diminish the responsibility of the board and senior management.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Outsourcing risk and an effective outsourcing risk programme. Explain, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 12.4, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: Elements of a service provider risk management programme
questions.question: A bank is preparing to outsource its retail loan collections process and is designing the governing programme. Which of the following is NOT an element of an effective service provider risk management programme as set out in the guidance?

options.text: Risk assessment of the activity before outsourcing, and due diligence covering the provider's business background, reputation, financial condition, operations and internal controls.
Contract provisions addressing scope, performance standards, reporting, audit rights, confidentiality, indemnification, default and termination, and dispute resolution.
Review of the service provider's incentive compensation arrangements, to check that they do not encourage imprudent risk taking on the institution's behalf.
Delegation of the ongoing oversight and monitoring function to the service provider itself, in order to preserve the independence of the institution's own control functions.

questions.solution:
Service provider risk management programme:

A. Risk assessments
B. Due diligence and selection of service providers
C. Contract provisions and considerations
D. Incentive compensation review
E. Oversight and monitoring of service providers
F. Business continuity and contingency considerations
G. Additional risk considerations

Element E is a function of the outsourcing institution. Delegating it to the provider would mean the provider assessing its own performance, which is the same self-review threat that prevents model developers from validating their own models and prevents internal audit from designing the framework it reviews. Oversight activity is expected to be commensurate with the level of risk and complexity of the relationship, and to include periodic review of the provider's financial condition, control environment, business continuity arrangements and compliance with contract terms.

Note also element F. The institution's own business continuity plan should address the failure or disruption of a critical service provider, and contracts should require the provider to maintain and test its own continuity arrangements and to report the results.

a.reason: Is an element, so not the answer. Elements A and B.

b.reason: Is an element, so not the answer. Element C.

c.reason: Is an element, so not the answer. Element D, and the one candidates most often forget because it looks like a human resources matter rather than a risk one.

d.reason: Not an element, and therefore the answer. Oversight and monitoring is retained by the institution.

trap.explanation: (d) is a role misassignment, and it is made attractive by a false independence argument, that keeping the institution's own control functions out of the relationship somehow preserves their objectivity. The opposite is true: independence here means independence from the provider, and self-monitoring by the provider is the definition of dependence. Option (c) is the memory hook worth taking away, since incentive compensation review is a named element that is easy to omit from a recalled list.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Outsourcing risk and an effective outsourcing risk programme. Explain, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 12.2, 12.4, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: Cross-border outsourcing
questions.question: A US bank is considering outsourcing its IT operations to a provider located in another country. Which of the following considerations is most important and specific to the cross-border nature of the arrangement?

options.text: The additional country risk arising from political, social, legal and economic conditions in the provider's jurisdiction, and whether the institution's and its supervisor's access to records, audit rights and data can be exercised there.
The likelihood that the offshore provider will charge less than a domestic one, which reduces the operational risk of the arrangement in proportion to the saving.
Whether the provider's home country is a member of the Basel Committee, since outsourcing to non-member jurisdictions is prohibited.
Whether the arrangement can be structured so that the provider's home supervisor assumes responsibility for the outsourced activity, thereby simplifying the institution's oversight burden.

questions.solution:
Foreign-based service providers introduce country risk on top of every risk that a domestic arrangement carries. The guidance directs institutions to consider the political, social, legal and economic conditions of the provider's jurisdiction, and to satisfy themselves that the arrangement does not impede their own ability, or their supervisor's ability, to obtain records and conduct examinations. Practical consequences include:

- Data protection and privacy law that may prevent transfer or inspection of customer data
- Enforceability of contract terms, including audit and termination rights, in the local courts
- Insolvency regimes that may determine what happens to the institution's data if the provider fails
- Continuity of service through local political or social disruption

The mitigants are contractual and operational rather than jurisdictional: express audit and access rights, provisions for supervisory access, data location and handling clauses, and a continuity plan that does not depend on the provider remaining operable.

b.reason: Cost saving is the commercial rationale for the arrangement and has no bearing on its operational risk. If anything, a materially cheaper provider warrants closer due diligence on how the saving is achieved.

c.reason: No such prohibition exists. Basel Committee membership is not a criterion for outsourcing eligibility.

d.reason: Supervisory responsibility does not transfer between jurisdictions, and the institution's own board and senior management remain responsible regardless of where the activity is performed.

trap.explanation: (c) is an absolute-claim trap, inventing a prohibition. (d) is a role misassignment, transferring supervisory responsibility across borders, and the offshore variant of the accountability fallacy seen elsewhere. (b) is a polarity flip, treating a cost reduction as a risk reduction. When a stem introduces a foreign provider, the examinable content is nearly always access: to records, to audit, to data, and to the provider's own regulators.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Third-party risk and an effective TPRM framework. Explain, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 13, Case Study: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.topic: Characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework
questions.question: A Chief Risk Officer is assessing the maturity of her firm's third-party risk management framework. Which of the following characteristics is most indicative of an effective framework?

options.text: A complete and maintained inventory of third parties, tiered by criticality, with due diligence, contractual protections, monitoring intensity and exit planning all scaled to the tier, and with fourth-party or subcontractor dependencies made visible.
A single annual questionnaire issued uniformly to every third party, so that all relationships are assessed to a consistent standard regardless of what they do.
A policy of contracting only with large, well-capitalised providers, since scale is the most reliable indicator that a provider will not fail.
Concentration of all critical services with one provider, so that oversight effort can be focused rather than dispersed across many relationships.

questions.solution:
Two principles run through the third-party material. The first is proportionality: not every third party matters equally, so the framework must tier relationships by criticality and scale every subsequent control to the tier. Applying identical treatment to a critical cloud provider and a stationery supplier wastes effort on the second and under-protects the first.

The second is visibility beyond the direct counterparty. Critical services are frequently subcontracted, so the institution's real dependency may sit with a party it has no contract with. Effective frameworks require disclosure of material subcontracting, cascade audit rights where appropriate, and map the dependency chain rather than the contract list.

```
Framework lifecycle:
   plan -> due diligence and selection -> contract -> ongoing
   monitoring -> termination and exit
```

Two failure modes the framework exists to prevent:
(i) an unmanaged critical dependency nobody inventoried
(ii) concentration, where many activities rest on one provider and the firm loses practical control over it

Note the definition of concentration risk used in this material is firm-level: the potential lack of control of an individual firm over a single provider as multiple activities are outsourced to it. That is what makes option (d) wrong rather than merely inefficient.

a.reason: Tiering, proportionate control, and subcontractor visibility.

b.reason: Uniform treatment is the opposite of proportionality. A single questionnaire cannot be simultaneously deep enough for a critical dependency and light enough to be worth issuing to a marginal one.

c.reason: Size is not a control. Large providers fail, suffer breaches and are themselves subject to concentration risk, and contracting exclusively with them tends to increase industry-wide concentration.

d.reason: This confuses concentrating oversight effort with concentrating exposure. Placing all critical services with one provider maximises exactly the concentration risk the framework is designed to control.

trap.explanation: (d) is a scope or condition error, and the designed trap, because its stated rationale, focusing oversight effort, is genuinely sensible administration attached to a structurally dangerous arrangement. (b) is a scope or condition error, replacing proportionality with uniformity and calling it consistency. (c) is a sibling swap, substituting a proxy for a control.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Third-party risk and an effective TPRM framework. Explain, describe
questions.reading: Chapter 13, Case Study: Third-Party Risk Management, and Chapter 5
questions.topic: Where third-party risk actually crystallises
questions.question: A bank suffers a major customer data breach. The intrusion originated with a contractor employed by the bank's cloud service provider, who exploited a misconfigured firewall in the provider's environment. Which of the following best describes the risk management conclusion to be drawn?

options.text: The bank's exposure was contractual only, since the failed control belonged to the provider and the bank had no ability to configure the provider's firewalls.

The bank remained ultimately responsible for the breach, which illustrates that outsourcing an activity places reliance on the provider's control environment without transferring accountability, and that the bank's monitoring should have extended to the provider's configuration and personnel controls.
The event should be classified as a credit risk exposure to the provider, since the loss arose from a counterparty's failure to perform.
The event demonstrates that cloud services should not be used for customer data, and the appropriate response is repatriation of all data to internal systems.

questions.solution:
This is the Capital One fact pattern, and the curriculum draws the conclusion explicitly: the hacker was a contractor at the cloud provider exploiting the provider's misconfigured firewalls, and Capital One was still ultimately responsible for the breach. Outsourcing is increasingly described as a risk sharing activity rather than a risk transfer activity, precisely because accountability is very difficult to transfer at all.

```
Before outsourcing: the firm runs the control, and bears the risk
                     of its own control failing.
After outsourcing:  the PROVIDER runs the control, and the firm bears
                     the risk of SOMEONE ELSE'S control failing,
                     with less visibility and less direct authority.
```

The exposure has changed shape. It has not gone away, and the accountability has not moved.

The practical implication is that monitoring must reach the controls the firm now depends on, which is why audit and inspection rights, evidence of the provider's own control testing, and visibility of subcontracted personnel are contractual requirements rather than negotiating luxuries.

Note the contrast the curriculum draws with the Equifax case. Capital One is treated as the example of a firm that responded well after the event, with prompt notification of law enforcement and regulators, public disclosure within ten days synchronised with the arrest, full application of the three Rs of crisis communication, tokenisation as an effective preventive control, and cyber liability insurance that may have offset some mitigation cost.

a.reason: Inability to configure the control does not extinguish responsibility for depending on it. The bank chose to place the data there.

c.reason: This is an operational loss arising from failed processes and systems at a third party, not a credit loss from a counterparty failing to repay an obligation.

d.reason: Reducing reliance on third parties is not the prescribed response anywhere in this curriculum. The response is to manage, map, contract around and monitor the dependency.

trap.explanation: (a) is a role misassignment, and it is seductive because its premise is factually true: the bank really could not configure that firewall. (c) is a sibling swap across risk disciplines, and worth noting because boundary events between operational and credit risk are separately examinable elsewhere. (d) is a scope or condition error, the manage-versus-eliminate reflex that is wrong in every objective in this document where it appears.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Evolution of stress testing; compare EBA, CCAR and SCAP. Describe, compare
questions.reading: Chapter 17, Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
questions.topic: What makes a crisis stress test credible
questions.question: A supervisor is designing a macro-prudential stress testing programme to restore market confidence in a banking system during a crisis. According to the reading, a successful programme has at least two components. Which of the following best identifies them?

options.text: A credible assessment of the capital strength of the tested institutions, sufficient to size the capital hole that needs to be filled; and a credible way of filling that hole.
A scenario severe enough to fail at least half the participating institutions; and a commitment not to disclose firm-level results, so that no institution is singled out.
A uniform capital hurdle applied identically across all jurisdictions; and a requirement that all participating banks use the same internal models.
A forward-looking horizon of at least five years; and the exclusion of sovereign exposures, which are risk-free by construction.

questions.solution:
Bank balance sheets are notoriously opaque and susceptible to asset substitution, that is the easy swapping of high risk for low risk assets, so stress tests tailored to the situation at hand can provide clarity by openly disclosing details of results and approaches, allowing trust to be regained. But disclosure alone is not enough.

- Component 1: a CREDIBLE ASSESSMENT of capital strength, so the market can size the capital hole.
- Component 2: a CREDIBLE WAY OF FILLING that hole, so the market knows the hole will actually be closed.

The 2009 US Supervisory Capital Assessment Program had both. The US entered 2009 with enormous uncertainty about the health of its banking system, and investors were reluctant to commit capital given the looming threat of possible government dilution. A credible loss assessment under a sufficiently stressful scenario let supervisors draw a line in the sand: fill this hole, and you will not risk being diluted later because the scenario was not tough enough. Behind it stood the Treasury's Capital Assistance Program, and the US Treasury was a sufficiently credible debt issuer that the CAP promise was itself credible.

Outcome: all banks with assets above USD 100 billion at year-end 2008 were included, accounting for two-thirds of total assets and about half of total loans in the US banking system. Ten of the 19 SCAP banks were required to raise USD 75 billion within six months and in fact raised USD 77 billion of Tier 1 common equity. None needed to draw on CAP funds, which is the clearest evidence the backstop worked by existing rather than by being used.

b.reason: Both halves are wrong. There is no target failure rate, and the reading treats greater disclosure as what restored credibility, not less. Withholding firm-level results is what made the 2010 European exercise less useful than the SCAP.

c.reason: Stress tests are tailored to the situation at hand, and the reading's whole point is that a bank's internal capital planning should reflect firm-specific factors rather than mirror the supervisor.

d.reason: Sovereign exposure was the central issue in the European tests, not an exclusion, and the criticism of the 2010 exercise was that haircuts were applied only to sovereign bonds held in the trading book when the bulk of the exposure sat in the banking book.

trap.explanation: (b) is a polarity flip on disclosure, and the most instructive wrong answer, because protecting individual institutions from disclosure is intuitively protective and was in practice corrosive to credibility. (d) is an absolute-claim trap on sovereign bonds being risk-free, which is exactly the assumption the eurozone crisis destroyed. The two-component test is worth memorising as a pair, because most exam framings of this objective turn on the second one, the backstop, which candidates forget.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Evolution of stress testing; compare EBA, CCAR and SCAP. Describe, compare
questions.reading: Chapter 17, Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
questions.topic: Comparing SCAP, the 2010 CEBS test and the 2011 EBA test
questions.question: An analyst is comparing the historical supervisory stress tests. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The 2010 CEBS exercise disclosed loss rates in more granular form than the SCAP, which is why markets reacted benignly to it.

The SCAP released loss rates by major asset class such as first-lien mortgages, credit cards and commercial real estate, whereas the 2010 CEBS exercise disclosed firm-level loss rates only for overall retail and overall corporate; the 2011 EBA test then disclosed far more, including exposure by asset class by geography and downloadable bank-level results.
The 2011 EBA test required a larger aggregate capital raise than the SCAP, which is why its disclosure was regarded as adequate.
All three exercises used an identical post-stress hurdle, so their results are directly comparable across jurisdictions and time.

questions.solution:
| | SCAP 2009 (US) | CEBS 2010 (Europe) | EBA 2011 (Europe) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coverage | 19 banks, all with assets above USD 100bn; two-thirds of total assets, about half of total loans | 91 banks; about two-thirds of total European bank assets and at least half in each participating country | 90 banks in 21 countries |
| Shortfall identified | 10 of 19 required to raise USD 75bn; USD 77bn raised | 7 of 91 required to raise EUR 3.5bn | 8 of 90 required to raise EUR 2.5bn |
| Disclosure | Loss rates by major asset class: first-lien mortgages, credit cards, commercial real estate and others | Firm-level loss rates for two sub-categories only: overall retail and overall corporate | Exposure by asset class by geography; all bank-level results downloadable in spreadsheet form |
| Backstop | Treasury Capital Assistance Program, credible and unused | None comparable | None comparable |
| Market reaction | Credibility restored | Benign, until Ireland requested assistance months later | Results no longer final: analysts could impose their own sovereign haircuts and re-test any of the 90 banks themselves |

The instructive sequence is that the two European exercises produced smaller headline shortfalls than the SCAP and yet were less credible. The 2010 test was followed by Irish banks that had all passed requiring EUR 24 billion on subsequent independent assessment by outside advisers. The 2011 test, despite far better disclosure, did nothing to alleviate concerns about the Spanish banking system, where five of 25 Spanish banks did not pass but the required additional raise netted to zero once provisions and mandatory bond conversions were taken into account. Spain was subsequently subject to an IMF FSAP and two further external exercises producing capital needs an order of magnitude larger.

a.reason: Disclosure was less granular than the SCAP, not more, and the benign market reaction proved short-lived.

c.reason: The 2011 EBA test required only EUR 2.5 billion, far less than the SCAP's USD 75 billion. Its disclosure was better despite, not because of, the small shortfall.

d.reason: Hurdles varied. The SCAP used a post-stress hurdle of 4% core Tier 1, and the later Spanish exercises used 4%, 6% and 7% core Tier 1 in different assessments, producing very different capital needs from the same banks.

trap.explanation: (c) is a wrong input twin in reasoning, substituting the size of the identified shortfall for the quality of the disclosure as the driver of credibility. (a) is a polarity flip on relative granularity. (d) is an absolute-claim trap on comparability, and the hurdle variation in the Spanish exercises is the cleanest disproof: the same banks needed EUR 17.7 billion at a 4% hurdle and EUR 37.1 billion at 7%.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Evolution of stress testing; compare EBA, CCAR and SCAP. Describe, compare
questions.reading: Chapter 17, Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann), and Chapter 20, Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: What supervisory stress testing became
questions.question: A newly appointed head of stress testing is explaining how the role of supervisory stress testing has evolved since 2009. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Broad-based supervisory stress testing became the new tool because standard approaches such as regulatory capital ratios were no longer credible during the crisis, and it evolved from a one-off crisis diagnostic into a recurring supervisory programme, in the United States through CCAR.
Stress testing replaced regulatory capital ratios entirely, so that a bank clearing its stress test no longer needs to meet minimum ratio requirements.
Because the crisis has passed, the cost-benefit balance of stress test disclosure has tipped decisively towards more bank-specific disclosure over time.

Supervisory stress tests are designed to provide an all-encompassing assessment of the risks a bank faces, which is why a bank's internal capital planning process should replicate the supervisory scenario and methodology.

questions.solution:
During the crisis, answers to the question of how much capital and liquidity a bank needs, obtained using standard approaches such as regulatory capital ratios, were no longer credible, and broad-based supervisory stress testing became the new tool. Because bank balance sheets are opaque and susceptible to asset substitution, a tailored stress test with open disclosure of results and approaches could restore trust in a way a ratio could not.

The 2009 SCAP was a crisis diagnostic. In the United States it became a recurring programme: CCAR is the Federal Reserve's supervisory programme for assessing capital plans, and in 2013 it covered the 18 BHCs that had participated in the 2009 SCAP. From 2014 the capital plans of all BHCs subject to the Capital Plan Rule were evaluated in a single unified process through CCAR.

Two qualifications matter. First, on disclosure, the reading's own view is that once trust is re-established the cost-benefit of stress testing disclosures may tip away from bank-specific towards more aggregated information, which is the opposite of option (c). Second, and examinably, the supervisory scenarios and stress tests required under the Dodd-Frank Act play an important role in CCAR but are not meant to be, and should not be viewed as, an all-encompassing assessment of the possible risks a BHC may face. A robust internal capital planning process should include modelling practices and scenario assumptions reflecting BHC-specific factors, which may differ considerably from the Federal Reserve's. Designing an internal capital planning process that simply seeks to mirror the Federal Reserve's stress testing is expressly described as a weak practice.

b.reason: Stress testing supplements minimum ratio requirements; it does not displace them. A bank must satisfy both.

c.reason: The direction is reversed. With trust re-established, the balance may tip towards more aggregated rather than more bank-specific information.

d.reason: Both halves are wrong, and this is the most examinable single sentence in the capital planning material: supervisory tests are not all-encompassing, and mirroring them is a weak practice.

trap.explanation: (d) is a scope or condition error, and the trap most likely to catch a practitioner, because building an internal process that tracks the supervisory one is operationally convenient and superficially prudent. The Federal Reserve names it as weak precisely because it substitutes the supervisor's judgement about a bank's risks for the bank's own. (c) is a polarity flip on the disclosure trajectory. (b) is an absolute-claim trap on replacement.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Capital Plan Rule and the seven CAP principles. Describe, explain
questions.reading: Chapter 20.1, Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: The Capital Plan Rule
questions.question: A regulatory affairs analyst is summarising the Federal Reserve's Capital Plan Rule for her firm's board. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The Rule requires all US-domiciled, top-tier bank holding companies with total consolidated assets of USD 50 billion or more to develop and maintain a capital plan supported by a robust process for assessing their capital adequacy, and CCAR is the supervisory programme through which those plans are assessed.
The Rule sets a minimum common equity Tier 1 ratio that BHCs must maintain and is enforced through the standardised approach to risk-weighted assets.
The Rule applies only to those BHCs that participated in the 2009 SCAP, and other institutions remain outside the capital planning regime.
The Rule prescribes the models a BHC must use to project losses and revenues, so that results are comparable across firms.

questions.solution:
The Capital Plan Rule requires all US-domiciled, top-tier BHCs with total consolidated assets of USD 50 billion or more to develop and maintain a capital plan supported by a robust process for assessing their capital adequacy. CCAR is the Federal Reserve's supervisory programme for assessing those capital plans. The Rule creates the obligation; CCAR is how compliance is examined.

The Federal Reserve's assessment of a BHC's capital planning process covers three things: the risk-identification, measurement and management practices that support capital planning and stress scenario analysis; stressed loss and revenue estimation practices; and the governance and controls around those practices. Note the emphasis, which the reading states directly: these initiatives focus not just on the amount of capital a BHC has, but on the internal practices and policies the firm uses to determine what amount and composition would be adequate.

The preamble to the Rule sets out the elements against which the Federal Reserve evaluates the robustness of internal capital planning, referred to as the capital adequacy process or CAP, and summarised as seven principles. In 2013 CCAR covered the 18 BHCs that had participated in the 2009 SCAP, with the remaining BHCs subject to the Rule assessed through a separate Capital Plan Review; from 2014 all were brought into a single unified CCAR process.

b.reason: Minimum ratios come from the capital rules, not the Capital Plan Rule. The Rule governs the planning process.

c.reason: SCAP participation determined which firms entered CCAR first, not who is subject to the Rule. The Rule's scope is the USD 50 billion asset threshold.

d.reason: The Rule does not prescribe models. The Federal Reserve expects BHC-specific modelling and scenario assumptions, and mirroring the supervisor is a weak practice.

trap.explanation: (b) is a sibling swap between the capital rules and the capital planning rule, and the easiest error to make because both concern capital. (c) is a scope or condition error, confusing the CCAR rollout population with the Rule's legal scope. (d) is a scope or condition error, and it contradicts the same principle tested elsewhere: the Rule demands a robust firm-specific process, not a standardised one.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Capital Plan Rule and the seven CAP principles. Describe, explain
questions.reading: Chapter 20, Figure 20.1, Capital Planning at Large Bank Holding Companies (Federal Reserve)
questions.topic: The seven principles of an effective capital adequacy process
questions.question: A BHC is self-assessing its capital adequacy process against the seven CAP principles. Which of the following is NOT one of those seven principles?

options.text: Sound foundational risk management
Effective loss-estimation methodologies
Comprehensive capital policy and capital planning
Independent third-party attestation of the capital plan

questions.solution:
| # | Principle | What it requires |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sound foundational risk management | Risk-measurement and risk-management infrastructure supporting the identification, measurement, assessment and control of all material risks arising from exposures and business activities |
| 2 | Effective loss-estimation methodologies | Processes for translating risk measures into estimates of potential losses over a range of stressful scenarios and environments |
| 3 | Solid resource-estimation methodologies | Processes for projecting the resources available to absorb losses, principally pre-provision net revenue and the allowance for loan and lease losses |
